**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**Surah al-Qari'ah (The Striking Calamity)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Striking Calamity!﴾ ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾.

The Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us) has already mentioned this at the beginning of Surah al-Waqi'ah, saying: "Like al-Tammah (the Overwhelming Calamity), al-Sakhkhah (the Deafening Blast), al-Azifah (the Approaching Event), and al-Qari'ah (the Striking Calamity)." End of quote. That is, likewise al-Sakhkhah and al-Sa'ah (the Hour).

It is well known that when a thing's importance is great, its names become numerous.

Or, as has been related from Imam 'Ali: "The multiplicity of names indicates the greatness of the one named."

It is also well known that these names are not synonyms, for each name indicates a meaning specific to itself.

So al-Waqi'ah is so named for the truth of its occurrence; al-Haqqah for the certainty of its occurrence; al-Tammah because it overwhelms and encompasses by its circumstances; and al-Azifah because of the nearness of its occurrence, ﴿The approaching event has drawn near﴾, like ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾. The same applies here.

They said: al-Qari'ah derives from the striking of a loud sound (qar' al-sawt al-shadid), because of the intensity of its terrors.

It was also said: al-Qari'ah is a name for severe hardship.

Al-Qurtubi said: The Arabs say, "The striking calamity struck them, and the breaking calamity broke them," when a dreadful matter befalls them.

Ibn Jarir said:

*"And a calamity from the days, were it not for their path, would have removed you for a while."*

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve for what they have done﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 31], and it is the most severe of the hardships of time.

As for His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾, it has already been mentioned that the statement of the scholars is that every occurrence of "wa ma adraka" (and what will make you know) means that it is made known to him, while every occurrence of "wa ma yudrika" (and what will make you know) means that it is not made known to him.

Here, He made it known by His saying: ﴿The Day when mankind will be like scattered moths, and the mountains will be like tufts of wool, fluffed up﴾ [Al-Qari'ah: 4-5]. This is one of its circumstances.

He also explained some of its other circumstances in al-Waqi'ah, that it is ﴿lowering [some] and raising [others]﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 3], and in al-Tammah and al-Sakhkhah: ﴿The man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾ [An-Naba': 40].

And His saying: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father﴾ [Abasa: 34-35].

Also, in every case where a state is mentioned, it is accompanied by the state that suits it. Since al-Qari'ah derives from qar', meaning striking, it fits that it be accompanied by that which weakens human strength to the feebleness of scattered moths, and dissolves the cohesion of mountains into the dust of fluffed-up wool.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 101, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾.

Al-Farash (moths) is the plural of farashah (a moth).

It is said: they are the ones that fly and hurl themselves into the fire.

It is also said: it is a delicate bird that seeks the fire and keeps rushing at the lamp or the like until it burns.

The Shaykh (al-Shinqiti) mentioned in his dictation the verse of Jarir:

"Indeed, al-Farazdaq, as far as I know, and his people are like moths that swarm around the fire of those who warm themselves."

Al-Farra' said: it is the swarming locusts that spread over the earth and climb upon one another from terror.

al-Qurtubi related from al-Farra' that it is the swarming gnats (hamaj) that fly, from mosquitoes and others.

From this comes al-jarad (locusts). It is said: he is more flighty than a farashah (moth). He said:

"A little one from a band of flighty ones, more flighty than the flying moth."

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My likeness and your likeness is like the likeness of a man who kindled a fire, and the locusts and moths began to fall into it, while he was driving them away from it. And I am holding you by your waistbands away from the Fire, and you are slipping away from my hand."

Al-mabthuth (scattered) means spread out.

A similar expression is His saying: ﴿They will come forth from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already explained this in the commentary on surah ﴿Iqtarabat al-sa'ah﴾, surah "Qaf wal-Qur'an", and surah ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ ﴿wal-Qur'an al-Hakim﴾, with sufficient detail that it need not be repeated here.

It has been said that describing them as moths refers to the first stage of their state, in confusion and bewilderment.

And describing them as locusts, in their multitude and unity of direction: ﴿hastening toward the caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8].

The author of the commentary says: ﴿And the mountains will be like wool, fluffed up.﴾

Earlier, the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and on us, explained in Surat al-Waqi'ah the states of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection, from their beginning as a heap of loose sand, then as fluffed-up wool, then as they move like a mirage.

In that place he referred to other passages, such as His saying: ﴿You think them solid, but they pass by like clouds pass by.﴾ [al-Naml: 88]

The reference to this was also given earlier, in Surat "Sa'ala sa'il" (al-Ma'arij).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 101, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾ ﴿he will be in a pleasing life﴾.

In His saying ﴿whose scales are heavy﴾ there is an indication of the weighing taking place for every person.

Al-Mawazin (the scales) may refer to the things weighed, and may refer to the instrument of weighing, like al-ma'ayir (the measures), and the two are mutually implicated.

It has already been stated that the measures are by the dharrah (the smallest particle) and less than it.

Texts have come concerning the setting up of the scales and their establishment with justice and equity.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, previously explained this at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything. And if there is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth, and sufficient are We as Accountants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47].

(p-73) As for His saying ﴿so he will be in a pleasing life﴾, they said: it means "a life that is pleasing" (mardiyyah), and radiyah (pleasing) originally is mardiyyah, as in His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful, pleased with their striving﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 8-9]. The attribution of being pleased to the life is because it is the one that performs the pleasing, since the word "life" comprises the bounties of Paradise and the causes of bounty, being content, obedient, and gentle toward the people of Paradise. Thus rivers are made to gush forth for them with ease, and fruits draw near with ease, as in His saying: ﴿Its fruit-clusters hang low﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23].

So the first view is the one known in rhetoric as the figure of speech of mentioning the place while meaning what is in it (idlaq al-mahall wa-iradat al-hall), as in His saying: ﴿Then let him call upon his council﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17].

Al-nadi (the council) is the place where a people gather, i.e., they call one another to assemble in it.

The meaning is: those who dwell in this council. Here the place has been named, which is the place of the life, and the one dwelling in it is intended.

On the second view: it is a genuine attribution of being pleased to the one who performs it or in whom it subsists. It is worth mentioning that taking it as a figure of speech (al-uslub al-bayani) is not appropriate as in the other verse, because the life is not a place for something else; rather it is something that dwells, and the true place is Paradise, while the life dwells in it, and it is a name for the meanings of bounty as previously stated. Therefore, taking the attribution literally is more correct.

Ahadith have come that Paradise feels for its people and rejoices in the doing of good, just as it adorns itself and rejoices in Ramadan, and that it contended with the Fire, and each boasted of its people and its joy in them, until Allah promised each of them that it would be filled.

The texts concerning the welcome by the houris, the youths, and the angels in Paradise to the people of Paradise with pleasure and greeting are well known.

And His saying: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57], i.e., nothing is withheld from them.

And His saying: ﴿And its keepers will say to them: "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it to abide therein"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

And His saying: ﴿Therein are women restricting their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [al-Rahman: 56].

Qasirat al-tarf (restricting their gaze) means restricting their gaze out of contentment with their husbands. From this is ﴿Houris, reserved in pavilions﴾ [al-Rahman: 72], i.e., reserved for their husbands.

(p-74) And His saying: ﴿And near over them will be its shade, and its fruit-clusters will be lowered in readiness﴾ [al-Insan: 14], and the like of that, which gives the sense that the bounty of Paradise itself is pleased with the people of Paradise. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

The Qur'anic verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for one whose scales are light﴾ ﴿his mother will be an abyss (Hawiyah)﴾.

There is disagreement about the intended meaning of His words ﴿his mother will be Hawiyah﴾. Does "his mother" mean his refuge, which is the Fire, and that Hawiyah is one of its names? Or does "his mother" mean his head, and Hawiyah derive from hawy (falling), so that he is thrown into the Fire headfirst, plunging into it?

Our teacher, may Allah have mercy on him, examined this matter in order to remove the appearance of contradiction. It is not far-fetched for someone to say that there is no contradiction between the two views.

So "his mother is Hawiyah" refers to the Fire, and he is thrown into it headfirst, his head plunging, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Al-Qurtubi related that "mother" carries the sense of Labid's verse:

*The earth is our refuge, and it was our mother, in it are our graves, and in it we are born.*

And in the sense of Hawiyah as a far-off depth and a calamity, is the poet's verse:

*O 'Amr, if our spears reached you, you would be like one whom the Hawiyah pulls down.*

Hawiyah means a place of falling.

As it has been said:

*I would eat blood if I do not make you bow to a co-wife, far-reaching in the fall of her earring, swaying of body.*

Or [she is] fragrant of scent.

In a hadith: "Indeed one of you speaks a word he sees no harm in, and it casts him into the Fire for seventy autumns."

We ask Allah for safety.

Hawiyah has been explained by what follows it: ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A blazing fire﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 10–11].

Hawiyah has also been explained as the lowest of the Fire's levels, we seek refuge in Allah.

Allah's words have also come: ﴿No! He will surely be thrown into the crusher. And what will make you know what the crusher is? The fire of Allah, kindled﴾ [al-Humazah: 4–6].

Al-nabdh means casting. This supports what we have said, that both meanings can be intended: his mother is Hawiyah, that is the Fire, into which he plunges upon his head, and this is by being cast into Hawiyah, which has a far-reaching fall. The habit of a body thrown from a great height is that the heaviest part precedes it downward, and the heaviest part of a human body is his head. And Allah knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book):

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-Qari'ah

The Qur'anic verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for one whose scales are light, his mother will be Hawiyah﴾.

This noble verse indicates that Hawiyah is a descriptive term and not a proper name for the Fire, since its being indefinite (tanwin) contradicts its being a name of the Fire, because if it were one of the names of the Fire it would be diptote (ghayr munsarif) due to proper-name status and feminine gender. And His words ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A blazing fire﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 10–11] indicate that Hawiyah is one of the names of the Fire.

First, know that there are three views among scholars regarding the meaning of His words ﴿his mother will be Hawiyah﴾. Two of them present no difficulty for the verse, and the third is the one in which the aforementioned difficulty lies.

As for the two views that present no difficulty for the verse: the first is that the meaning is ﴿his mother will be Hawiyah﴾, that is, the mother of his head will be an abyss in the bottom of Hell, because he will be cast into it with his head downward and his feet upward. This view was related from Qatadah, Abu Salih, Ikrimah, al-Kalbi and others. According to this view, the pronoun in His words ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ refers to an omitted antecedent indicated by the context, meaning: the mother of his head will be an abyss in a fire, ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A blazing fire﴾.

The second: it is from the Arabic usage when they invoke ruin upon a man, saying: "May his mother fall (hawat ummuh)," because when he falls, that is, he is destroyed, his mother has fallen, bereaved and grieving. From this meaning is the verse of Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi:

*May his mother fall, what the morning brings forth as it goes, and what the night returns with when it comes back.*

This view is another narration from Qatadah. According to this view, the pronoun in His words "it" (hiyah) refers to the calamity (ad-da'hiyah) indicated by the discourse. Al-Alusi mentioned in his tafsir that the author of al-Kashshaf said this view is the best, and al-Tibi said it is the most evident, while he himself said: "There is room for discussion about it."

The third, which contains the difficulty: the meaning is ﴿his mother will be Hawiyah﴾, that is, his refuge which encloses him, and in his embrace is Hawiyah, which is the Fire, because a mother shelters her child and embraces him, and the Fire embraces this disobedient one and becomes his refuge.

The answer to this view is what al-Alusi indicated in his tafsir, that He made Hawiyah indefinite in a position where definiteness would be expected, to indicate that it has departed from what is known, for magnification and awe. Then, after making it vague for this purpose, He clarified it by its awe-inspiring description in His words ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A blazing fire﴾.

The author, may Allah pardon him, said: This answer given by al-Alusi falls within a type of rhetorical embellishment (badi') in its semantic branch, which the scholars of rhetoric call *tajrid* (abstraction). The definition of tajrid according to them is that one extracts from a thing possessing a quality another similar to it in that quality, as exaggeration of its perfection in it. Its types are well known among the scholars of eloquence (bayan). Among them is tajrid by means of a particle, as in the saying: "I have from so-and-so a warm friend (sadiq hamim)," meaning he has reached such a degree of friendship that it is valid to extract from him another similar to him in it, exaggerating its perfection in him. And the saying: "If you ask him, you will indeed ask of him the sea," he exaggerated in his attribute of generosity until he extracted from him a sea of generosity. Among tajrid through a particle is His words ﴿For them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ [Fussilat: 28], which is the most similar thing to the verse we are dealing with, because the Fire is precisely the abode of eternity, but He extracted from it another abode and made it prepared in Hell for the disbelievers, to magnify its matter and exaggerate its attribute of severity. Among tajrid is that which occurs without the mediation of a particle, as in the saying of Qatadah ibn Salamah al-Hanafi:

*And if I remain, I will certainly set out on a raid that gathers spoils, or a noble man will die.*

He means himself: he extracted from himself a noble man, exaggerating his generosity. So when you know this, the Fire was called Hawiyah because of the extreme depth of it and the distance of its fall. It has been related that one who falls into it falls for seventy autumns, and some have specified it as the lowest gate of the Fire, and extracted from it another Hawiyah similar to it in extreme depth and distance of fall, exaggerating its depth and the distance of its fall. And Allah knows best.
